title: Noor and the Blue Hour
premise: Kestrel Marchetti, night librarian in a city that never fully darkens, has spent fifteen years guarding a secret: a song she wrote for her brother Theo before he vanished, a song never recorded, never sung. When it drifts out of a late-night radio, performed by a street musician named Noor, Kestrel realizes someone who knew Theo is alive and talking. Following the song through the city's sleepless underbelly, she uncovers the truth of what Theo did to survive and what it cost the people who loved him, and must decide whether justice belongs to the law, to memory, or to the living. In the end, she sings the song aloud at last—naming him, naming herself—and lets the recording exist, choosing belonging over invisibility even as the last person who could confirm her story slips away.
about_author: Lena Blackwood is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent a decade collecting the stories of people who call in at 3 a.m. She writes about the hours when cities pretend to sleep and the things people only say when they believe no one is listening.

chapters.title: The Hour That Doesn't Count
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A night in the library's blue hour, cataloging lost-and-found objects and practicing her ritual of almost-saying things aloud to empty reading rooms. We learn Theo vanished fifteen years ago and she's never spoken his name since. Emotional beat: the comfort and suffocation of invisibility.

chapters.title: Static, Then a Voice
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Driving home at dawn, the radio plays a song she wrote for Theo—unrecorded, known to no one living. The performer is credited only as 'Noor.' She tracks the station; the DJ barely remembers the drop-in. Emotional beat: vertigo, the past arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: The Man Who Sings Other People's Songs
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. A busker in the transit tunnels who learned songs from a dying man in a squat years ago and promised to keep them alive. He doesn't know their origins. Emotional beat: the ethics of carrying someone else's voice, and his loneliness mirrored against Kestrel's.

chapters.title: Everything Theo Told Me Was a Story
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She confronts Noor, who describes 'a man called Finch'—Theo's street name—and the winter they shared. But his account of Theo's final months contradicts the official record. Emotional beat: grief complicated by the realization she never knew her brother's whole life.

chapters.title: The Case That Closed Itself
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, with a flashback to Detective Ilsa Vann. Kestrel pulls Theo's file: ruled accidental, closed in eleven days, one witness statement she's never seen—signed by someone named R. Okonkwo. Emotional beat: suspicion hardening into purpose; the law's indifference to the invisible.

chapters.title: Rosa
chapters.summary: Rosa Okonkwo's POV. A former social worker who witnessed something the night Theo died and traded her silence for her family's safety, carrying the weight ever since. She recognizes Kestrel instantly but lies. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid in installments over fifteen years.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Noor's POV, alternating. Following Theo's last known route through the river district, they find the squat, a hidden notebook of his songs, and evidence he witnessed something he shouldn't have. Emotional beat: rising dread—Theo didn't just vanish; he was erased.

chapters.title: The Confession at 4 A.M.
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Rosa calls the late-night radio show—the same one that aired Noor—and confesses on air: a powerful man's fixer killed Theo; she was threatened into silence. Kestrel hears it live. Emotional beat: catharsis and terror; justice finally spoken, but outside any courtroom's reach.

chapters.title: Blue Hour, Sung
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The man responsible is dying; the law will never touch him. At the river where Theo was found, Kestrel performs the song aloud for the first time, with Noor and Rosa present, naming her brother and herself. Emotional beat: climax—grief transmuted into witness, the price of survival finally named.

chapters.title: Daylight Hours
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, epilogue a year later. The recorded song circulates; Theo's notebook is archived in her library under his real name. Kestrel takes a daytime shift, teaches a songwriting workshop, and visits Rosa, who has begun telling the truth in smaller ways. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, invisibility set down like a coat no longer needed.
